segs.text: In this lesson, you will learn the basic words for defensive work, and how to give a fielder clear instructions in English.
You already know how to teach defense. The goal here is to say it the way an American coach says it: short, direct and easy to follow.
Start with the ready position. That is the athletic stance a fielder is in when the ball reaches the hitting zone.
To ask for it, say: get in your ready position. Or simply: get ready.
Then add one cue at a time. Stay low. Glove out front.
Notice the word your. In English, a coach says bend your knees, not bend the knees. It sounds personal, and it sounds like a coach.
Now the core words. The glove. Footwork, which means how the feet move.
You field a ground ball. Field the ball, and then you throw.
You catch a fly ball, or a throw. Catch it with two hands.
And throw is the word for every fielder. Pitch is only for the pitcher.
On the field, American coaches use short commands. A verb, and two or three words. Stay low. Move your feet.
Keep your eyes on the ball. Take your time.
This is normal, and it is not rude. A player needs one clear cue between reps, not a long sentence.
You do not need please in every cue. On the field, it can sound strange. The warmth comes from your tone, the player's name, and honest praise.
Off the field, with staff or in a meeting, softer forms are more common: can you, or would you mind.
You can also soften a correction. Start with what went well, then give the cue. Nice. Now stay low.
Let's makes it a team effort. Let's try it again.
After a mistake, send him back calmly. Reset. Take your time.
And when he gets it right, tell him right away. That's it. One more.
Listen to Coach Ramírez with Tyler, a shortstop. First, an instruction before the rep.
Tyler, get in your ready position. Stay low, and keep your eyes on the ball.
Now, a correction after the rep.
Good hands. Your feet stopped there. Move your feet to the ball. Try again.
Notice what he did. Before the rep, two short cues. After the rep, something good, one problem, one fix, and then back to work.
Finally, check that the player understood. Almost every player answers yes to do you understand. Better questions get real answers.
Even better, ask him to do it. Show me.
Or ask him to describe the rep. What did you feel there?
A quick, informal check is: you with me?
Then listen to the answer. If he says, I came up early, he felt it himself, and your next cue will make sense to him.
Let's review. One short cue before the rep. One simple correction after it. Then check that he understood.
Next, you will listen to two short moments from practice, build sentences, and then coach Tyler through a ground ball yourself.
OK, guys, line up at short. Today we're working on ground balls.
Yes. Field the ball, then throw to first. But first, ready position. Stay low, and glove out front.
Let's do eight each. Take your time. I want clean reps, not fast reps.
Good effort, Jake. What did you feel there?
I think I came up too early. I lost the ball.
Right. Stay low until the ball is in your glove, and keep your eyes on it. Does that make sense?
OK. Show me. Reset, and let's try it again.
Coach, what should I focus on this rep?
I don't know, Coach. That one felt weird.
Stay low, and keep your eyes on the ball.
Nice. Now move your feet. Does that make sense?
I'm ready, Coach. Anything you want me to work on?
Got it, Coach. Hit me one.
Sorry, Coach, I didn't catch that. What do you want me to focus on?
How was that? I think I came up a little early.
OK, I'll fix that on the next one.
Sorry, what should I change on the next one?
Yeah, I'm with you. Here we go.
Sorry, Coach. Should I go now, or wait?
In the last lesson, you gave short, clear instructions. In this one, you will add the words for footwork, positioning and throwing.
You will also learn to explain why an adjustment helps. A player who understands the reason usually remembers the cue.
Defense starts with the first step. Its direction matters as much as its speed. Good first step. Your first step was late.
The angle is the path he takes to the ball. Take a better angle.
When a player waits for the ball, say: get your feet moving.
Notice the verb take. In English, you take a step, you take an angle, and you take a ball on the backhand.
Now, side to side. The glove side is the side of the glove hand.
A ball on the glove side is a forehand. Open glove, palm to the ball.
A ball on the other side is a backhand. The shortstop's play in the hole is a backhand. Take it on the backhand.
The hole is the space between the shortstop and the third baseman.
Here is the play from the ball to the throw. Work through the ball. Keep moving toward the throw. Don't stop on it.
The transfer is the ball going from the glove to the throwing hand. Quick transfer.
Set your feet before you throw.
And the throwing lane is a clear line to the target, with no runner in the way. Clear your lane.
A command tells the player what to do. A short reason tells him why. Put the reason after the cue, and keep it short.
Use so you. Set your feet, so you can make a strong throw.
Use because. Take a better angle, because it saves you a step.
Or use that gives you. Play a step in. That gives you more time.
Keep the reason honest. If you are not sure an adjustment will help, say: let's try it and see how it feels.
Good feedback keeps two things apart: what you saw, and what to try.
Start with what you saw. I saw your feet stop before the throw. I noticed you rounded that ball.
Then give one thing to try. Try a quicker first step. Let's try it with your feet set.
I saw, and try, are two short patterns. You can use them with any skill, even when your English is still growing.
Positioning is where a fielder stands before the pitch. To shade means to move a few steps to one side. Listen to Coach Ramírez with Jake, his second baseman.
Jake, shade two steps toward the middle. This hitter goes up the middle a lot, so that gives you a better angle on those balls.
Two steps toward the bag. Got it.
And talk to Tyler, so he knows where you are.
Notice the last line. Communication is part of positioning. When one fielder moves, the fielder next to him needs to know.
Let's review. One cue, one short reason. What you saw, then what to try. And when the work is good, keep it going. Let's do three more.
Next, you will listen to a drill and a positioning conversation, build sentences, and then walk Jake through a drill yourself.
OK, Tyler, Jake. Next drill: forehands and backhands. I roll it to one side, you get your feet moving.
Do we throw after each one?
Yes. Field it, quick transfer, set your feet, then throw to Jake at second. Set your feet first, so the throw is on line.
Six each side. Last one is a backhand in the hole.
Coach, what are you working on with Tyler today?
His angle. I saw him round a lot of balls to his right, so he's late on the throw.
What are you having him try?
A quicker first step, and a better angle. That gives him a shorter path, and he can work through the ball to first.
Makes sense. Is he getting it?
Better every day. We'll do three more rounds tomorrow.
Coach, why do you want me to take a different angle?
What did you see on that one?
Set your feet before you throw.
Get your body behind it, so the ball stays in front of you.
Take a better angle. Let's do three more.
Morning, Coach. What's the drill today?
Sorry, Coach, can you say that again? What are we doing?
Before we start, where do you want me to play this hitter?
Got it. I'll let Tyler know where I am.
Wait, which way do you want me to move, and why?
I got to that one, but my throw went high. What happened?
OK, that makes sense. I'll try it.
Sorry, I didn't get that. What should I do differently?
Sorry, Coach. How many more do you want?
Welcome to your first lesson. In the next few minutes, you will learn how to introduce yourself in English, ask a few simple questions, and keep a short conversation going.
You can pause at any time. Tap a sentence to hear it again, and press the microphone to practice it yourself.
First, just listen. Carlos is a coach at the academy. Emily is a new analyst. They are meeting for the first time.
Hi, my name is Carlos. I'm from Santo Domingo.
Nice to meet you, Carlos. I'm Emily. What do you do?
I'm a baseball coach. I work with young players.
How long have you been coaching?
Let's look at the greetings. Hi, and hello, are both fine with anyone. Hi is a little more relaxed.
In the morning, you can say: good morning.
When you meet someone for the first time, say: nice to meet you.
And the answer is: nice to meet you too.
Now, five short patterns to talk about yourself.
I am, or I'm. I'm Carlos. I'm a coach.
I'm from. I'm from Santo Domingo.
I work. I work with young players.
I have. I have two children.
And I usually, for things you do most days. I usually arrive at seven.
One important detail. In Spanish, you can say trabajo, without yo. In English, you always need the subject. Say: I work. Not just: work.
Conversations need questions. Here are three you will use every day.
How are you? A good answer is: I'm good, thanks. And you?
Where are you from? I'm from Baní.
What do you do? This question is about your job. I'm a pitching coach.
Notice the small question at the end: and you? It sends the conversation back to the other person. It is polite, and it keeps the conversation going.
Now, three mistakes that Spanish speakers often make. Knowing them will make your English sound much more natural.
First, age. In Spanish you say tengo treinta años. In English, say: I'm thirty years old. Or just: I'm thirty.
Second, time doing something. Say: I've been coaching for four years. Or, more simply: about four years.
Third, jobs. In English you need a before the job. I'm a coach. I'm a pitching coach. Before a vowel sound, use an: I'm an analyst.
In real conversations, people speak fast. That is normal. Here are three sentences that will save you.
Can you speak more slowly, please?
And: what does that mean? Asking is not a weakness. Good communicators check that they understood.
Listen to one more short conversation. Mike is a hitting coach visiting the academy.
Pretty good. Do you work here every day?
Yes. I usually arrive at seven, and practice starts at eight.
Carlos answers the question, and then he adds a little more information. That is a great habit. A short answer plus one extra detail makes you sound natural and friendly.
Let's review. Say your name and where you are from. Say what you do. Ask a question back.
Next, you will practice these sentences, listen to two conversations, and then speak with a new colleague. Take your time. Making mistakes is part of learning.
Hi! Are you one of the coaches?
Yes. Hi, my name is Carlos. I'm from Santo Domingo.
Nice to meet you, Carlos. I'm Emily. I'm from Texas.
Nice to meet you too. What do you do?
I'm a performance analyst. I work with the video and the numbers.
Great. I'm a baseball coach. I work with young players, mostly infielders.
How long have you been coaching?

Hi everyone, I'm Mike. I'm the new hitting coach. I'm from Chicago, and I have two kids. I usually get to the field at seven thirty. My Spanish is not very good yet, so please be patient with me. I'm happy to be here!
Hi, I'm Emily. What's your name, and where are you from?
What do you usually do in the morning at the academy?
Hi, my name is Carlos. I'm from Santo Domingo.
Nice to meet you. What do you do?
Hi! I don't think we've met. I'm Emily, the new analyst.
Nice to meet you! Where are you from?
Oh, nice. And what do you do here?
Cool. How long have you been coaching?
That's great. Well, I have a meeting now. It was nice meeting you. See you at practice!
In this lesson, you will learn how to give a player simple instructions during practice: what to do, how to do it, and how to encourage him.
You already know the baseball. The goal is to say it clearly in English, with short sentences a player understands right away.
In English, an instruction usually starts with the verb. There is no you at the beginning.
These are not rude. On a baseball field, this is the normal, clear way to talk. Your tone does the rest.
Instructions often point to a part of the body. Hands. Feet. Knees. Chest. Glove hand.
Or to a direction. Forward. Back. Left. Right. Stay low. Work through the ball.
Or to equipment. Grab your glove. Put the balls in the bucket. Line up at the cone.
You will also tell players where to go.
Come in, means move closer. Back up, means move back.
And when players change places: switch with Tyler.
To explain a short drill, put the steps in order with three small words: first, then, and after that.
First, field the ball in front of you.
Then, move your feet toward first base.
After that, make a good throw.
And to set the number of reps, use let's. Let's do five more.
Listen to Coach Dave working with Tyler, a young shortstop.
OK, Tyler, today we're working on your first step. Stay low, and watch the ball into your glove.
Good. Your feet stopped on that one. Keep your feet moving through the ball. Try it again.
That's it! Much better. Let's do five more.
Notice what Coach Dave did. He said what they were working on. He gave one correction. And he encouraged the player.
To check understanding, ask: do you understand what we're working on? Or simply: show me.
To correct, start with something positive, then give one clear change. Good. Now keep your glove out in front.
And to encourage: nice job. That's it. Much better.
Sometimes you need to say what not to do. Use don't, plus the verb.
But here is a coaching tip. A player understands faster when you say what to do. Instead of don't drop your glove, say: keep your glove out in front.
You will also hear short expressions from American coaches. You don't have to use them all, but you should understand them.
Reset means go back to your starting position.
Stay through it means keep the movement going to the end.
And attaboy means great job. It is friendly and very common.
If your English is a little stronger, add the reason. Use so, or because.
Stay low, so you can see the ball longer.
Keep your head still, because it helps your eyes track the ball.
Now it's your turn. Practice the instructions, listen to a coach explain a drill, and then run a short drill yourself.
Alright guys, bring it in. This drill is called short hops. Grab your glove and line up at the cone.
First, I roll you a ball. Stay low and field it in front of you. Then, move your feet and throw to the bucket at second base.
We'll do ten each. Take your time, and watch the ball all the way into your glove. Any questions?
Hey Tyler, nice effort on that one. Your glove was good, but your head moved. Keep your head still and watch the ball. OK? Show me.
Yes! That's it. Much better. Let's do three more.
Keep your head still and watch the ball.
Do you understand what we're working on?
Nice job. Let's do five more.
Coach, what are we working on today?
Coach, I keep missing the ball. What am I doing wrong?
Hey Coach! What are we doing today?
OK. How many do we do?
How was that one? I think my feet stopped.
Got it. Should I go again?
Stay low and move your feet.
In this lesson, you will learn to talk about grips in Spanish: the fingers, the seams, where the fingers go, and how much pressure to use.
You already know grips. The goal here is to explain one small adjustment clearly, and then ask the pitcher what he feels.
You will hear Coach Alex, a bilingual pitching coach, and Luis, a nineteen-year-old pitcher from the Dominican Republic. Repeat each Spanish line out loud when you hear it.
Start with the hand. Spanish names every finger, so you can be exact.
el dedo medio… el dedo del medio
Then the parts of the hand you will mention most in grip work.
la palma, la muñeca, las yemas de los dedos
On the field, many players simply say the tips of the fingers.
You will also hear this word. It also means a ball in the count, so for the object in his hand, the first word is clearer.
The horseshoe is the U-shaped part of the seams. It gives you a quick way to name the seam you mean.
Here is a four-seam grip. The pitch is called…
Listen to Coach Alex describe where the fingers go.
Pon los dedos sobre las costuras.
El índice y el medio, encima de la herradura.
El pulgar, debajo de la pelota.
Notice that Spanish says the fingers, not your fingers. With parts of the body, that is normal, and it does not sound cold.
Pitch names mix Spanish and English. That is normal in Dominican baseball, and in Spanish-language baseball media.
el sinker, el slider, el cutter
These English names are usually masculine. You may hear the feminine too, and either will be understood. Some pitches also have a Spanish name.
And for the session itself, the English word stays.
Between pitches, short instructions are normal. Start with the verb, then the finger or the grip.
Listen to the small words at the end: a little, a tiny bit. They soften the instruction. It sounds like an adjustment you are trying together, not a mistake he made.
Spanish has two ways to say you. The informal one is normal with young academy players.

The formal one is for older or veteran players, staff and parents, or when you are not sure. That is guidance, not a fixed rule. Players may address you formally even when you speak informally to them.
In instructions, the formal form usually changes the last vowel. Listen to each pair.
If you are unsure which one a player prefers, ask him. It is a respectful question.
The changeup has two names. Both are standard.
el cambio… el cambio de velocidad
Pressure is part of the grip too.
And depth: is the ball deep in the hand, or out in the fingertips?
más adentro en la mano… en la punta de los dedos
Finally, the moment the ball leaves the hand.
Now listen to Coach Alex with Luis during a bullpen. Alex suggests one change, then asks how it feels.
Luis, separa un poco los dedos. Así.
Cómodo. Un poco raro, pero cómodo.
After the pitch, ask about the release.
La sentí mejor en los dedos.

One change, then a question. His answer tells you whether to keep the adjustment or try something else. Next, you will practise these words, build sentences, and then coach Luis through a grip change yourself.
Luis, vamos a empezar con la recta de cuatro costuras.
El índice y el medio sobre la herradura. El pulgar, debajo de la pelota.
Eso. Ahora separa un poquito los dedos y tira cinco rectas.
Coach, el cambio se me queda arriba.
Bien fuerte, en la punta de los dedos.
Vamos a probar algo. Ponla más adentro en la mano y afloja un poco el agarre.
Tira tres. Después me dices cómo se siente.
Pon los dedos sobre las costuras. Separa un poco los dedos.
¿Cómo se siente ese agarre? ¿Qué sentiste cuando soltaste la pelota?
Coach, este agarre lo siento muy apretado.
Coach, ¿cómo quieres que agarre la pelota?
Perdón, coach, no te entendí. ¿Dónde pongo los dedos?
Siento los dedos muy juntos. ¿Los dejo así?
¿Y el pulgar? Lo tengo al lado de la pelota.
Listo, coach. Ya tiré con el agarre nuevo.
Se siente cómodo. La pelota salió mejor de los dedos.
In this lesson, you will learn to talk about the delivery in Spanish: balance, direction, the hips and shoulders, the stride, the arm, and the release.
More important, you will learn how to say it: describe what you saw on one pitch, ask what he felt, and suggest one adjustment to test.
Start with the body. Listen and repeat.
Now the delivery, from start to finish.
The second word is correct but formal. With players, the first is more common.
el brazo… el ángulo del brazo
With players, describing it is often clearer.
The most useful frame in coaching Spanish means let's. It makes the work something you do together.
Vamos a trabajar en tu balance.
For one short cue before a pitch, an instruction is fine.
Mantén la dirección hacia el plato.
After a rep, describe what you saw on that pitch. Start with: I noticed, or, it looked to me like.
Me pareció que el lado de adelante se abrió temprano en ese lanzamiento.
The verb is in the past. It happened on that pitch. You are describing one rep, not judging the pitcher.
Now compare it with this sentence.
Siempre tienes que mantener el lado de adelante cerrado.
Always, and have to. That turns one observation into a universal rule. Mechanics are individual, and no single cue is right for every pitcher, so experienced coaches avoid this kind of sentence.
Vamos a probar mantener el lado de adelante cerrado un poquito más.
¿Qué tal si apuntas el pie hacia el cátcher?
Or give him something outside the body to focus on.
Fíjate en el guante del cátcher.
After the rep, check the feel, and let him locate the release himself.
Keep changes small, one at a time, and part of the plan you share with the rest of the staff. Ask about discomfort, and never push a change that hurts.
Here is an illustrated rep. It is a drawing, not a real pitcher, and not a diagnosis. In this drawing, the front side opens early.
Listen to how Coach Alex talks about it: what he saw, then a question.
En ese lanzamiento, me pareció que el lado de adelante se abrió temprano.
Sentí que el brazo llegó un poco tarde.
Vamos a probar algo. Fíjate en el guante del cátcher y mantén el hombro de adelante cerrado un poquito más.
In the second drawing, the front side stays closed a little longer. Coach Alex describes it and checks the feel.
Ahí se quedó cerrado un poquito más. ¿Sentiste alguna diferencia?
Sí, sentí el brazo más suelto.
Bien. Vamos a revisar el video, y después prueba ese ajuste otra vez.
Describe what happened, ask what he felt, suggest one thing to test, and say what you will check on the next rep. That is exactly what you will do in the conversation at the end of this lesson.
Luis, hoy vamos a trabajar en tu balance. Nada más eso.
Sí, diez rectas. Fíjate en el guante del cátcher y mantén la dirección hacia el plato.
Coach, yo voy a grabar el video desde el lado.
Perfecto, Ana. Después lo revisamos juntos, Luis.
No sé, coach. Sentí que el brazo llegó tarde.
Me pareció que el lado de adelante se abrió un poco temprano. Vamos a revisar el video.
Aquí está, coach. Mira el hombro de adelante.
Sí. ¿Qué tal si mantienes el hombro cerrado un poquito más? Prueba ese ajuste en las próximas tres.
Noté que el lado de adelante se abrió temprano en ese lanzamiento.
¿Sentiste alguna diferencia? Prueba ese ajuste otra vez.
Ah, ok. ¿El lado de adelante se abrió temprano?
Perdón, coach, no te entendí. ¿Qué pasó en esa?
Sentí que el brazo llegó un poco tarde.
¿Y qué hago diferente en la próxima?
Listo, coach. ¿En qué me fijo en esta?
Ok. Después te digo si sentí la diferencia.
Perdón, coach, ¿en qué me tengo que fijar?
Hi, I'm Anna. I'm from Miami. I work with the pitchers.
Practice starts at eight thirty tomorrow.
Hey, the bus to the game leaves at one, not at two. Please tell the players to be in the parking lot by twelve forty-five.
Coach, can I hit in the first group today?
Not today. You're in the second group, after the infield work.
So the plan for this week is to cut back on live batting practice. A lot of the guys are getting tired, so we'll do more tee work and front toss, and we'll go back to live BP on Friday.
Honestly, his effort is great, but he's still rushing his throws. I'd like to slow him down before we move him to shortstop.

I don't think the issue is his arm strength. If you look at the video, he's catching the ball late and then trying to make up for it, which is why the throws sail. Clean up the exchange and the accuracy will follow.
I hear you, but I'm not sure we can afford to sit him for two weeks. Let's check in with the medical staff before we make that call.
Tell me your name, where you're from, and what you do.
What time do you usually arrive at the academy?
Explain what you normally do at work in the morning.
Hey Coach, what time does practice start tomorrow? And where do we meet?
One of your players keeps making the same mistake in practice. What would you tell him, and why?
Some coaches want shorter practices and more video sessions. What do you think about that idea? Explain your opinion.
Okay, ready position. Feet wide, knees bent, glove out front.
Your first step was late. Read it off the bat and go. And set your feet before you throw.

Good rep. Your glove was out front, and that's exactly what we wanted. The only thing is you came up a little early, so the ball got under your glove. Let's do three more, and this time see it all the way into the glove.
Coach, I'm up next. Anything I should do on this ground ball?
Coach, what should I focus on during this drill?
Hola, soy Ana. Soy de Puerto Plata. Trabajo en la oficina del equipo.
La reunión es mañana a las nueve y media.
Muchachos, el autobús sale a la una, no a las dos. Estén en el estacionamiento a las doce y cuarenta y cinco.
Pollo, por favor. No me gusta mucho el pescado.
Esta semana vamos a cambiar el horario porque hace demasiado calor por la tarde. Empezamos a las siete de la mañana y terminamos antes del mediodía.
Ana, te llamo porque se me quedó el pasaporte en el hotel. ¿Puedes decirle al chofer que me espere unos diez minutos?

No creo que el problema sea la falta de interés. Lo que pasa es que las clases de inglés coinciden con el entrenamiento, así que muchos jugadores no pueden ir. Si las pasáramos a la noche, seguramente vendrían más.
Antes de decidir si juega el domingo, prefiero hablar con el personal médico. No quiero arriesgarlo por un solo partido.
Luis, ahora tira el cambio. Tres lanzamientos.
Mueve el pulgar un poquito más debajo de la pelota. Así. ¿Se siente natural?
Bien, pero la sentí un poco resbalosa en los dedos.
Ok. Sécate la mano y tira otra igual.

Me fijé que en los últimos cambios estás soltando la pelota un poco antes y se te quedan arriba. No creo que sea el agarre; me parece que estás apurando el brazo. Probemos con el mismo ritmo de la recta, a ver qué pasa.
Dime tu nombre, de dónde eres y a qué te dedicas.
¿A qué hora llegas normalmente al trabajo?
Explícame qué haces normalmente en el trabajo por la mañana.
Coach, ¿a qué hora empieza la práctica mañana? ¿Y dónde nos reunimos?
Uno de tus jugadores comete el mismo error en cada práctica. ¿Qué le dirías y por qué?
Algunos entrenadores quieren prácticas más cortas y más sesiones de video. ¿Qué opinas de esa idea? Explica tu opinión.
Coach, ¿cómo agarro la recta? ¿Dónde pongo los dedos?
stride direction / line to the plate
la separación de cadera y hombros
trabaja a través de la bola
mira la bola hasta el guante
keep your eyes on the ball
no le quites la vista a la bola
